source_refs.note: Book p. 202-203: 11.2 even and odd functions, two Remember! boxes, unit-circle figure for cos and sin, Note box. Print slips: (-x)^2 = x, (-x)^3 = -x, missing '=' and 'f', 'figure 9.2'. Teaching notes, Key points, Common mistakes ours.

blocks.text: A function \(f\) is said to be even if \(f(-x) = f(x)\), for every number \(x\) in the domain of \(f\).

blocks.title: Remember!
blocks.text: The graph of an even function is always symmetric about the \(y\)-axis.

For example: \(f(x) = x^{2}\) is an even function of \(x\). Here
\(f(-x) = (-x)^{2} = x = f(x)\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In this part the book's print has slips: the definition line misses the sign "=" between \(f(-x)\) and \(f(x)\), and the example prints \((-x)^{2} = x\). The correct lines are:
\[f(-x) = f(x)\]
\[f(-x) = (-x)^{2} = x^{2} = f(x)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Even means: changing the sign of the input does not change the output. Test it with numbers for \(f(x) = x^{2}\):
\[f(3) = 9, \qquad f(-3) = 9\]
Because of this, the point \((3, 9)\) and its mirror point \((-3, 9)\) are both on the graph. Folding the graph along the \(y\)-axis, the two halves fall on each other: that is the symmetry in the Remember! box.
A function \(f\) is said to be odd if \(f(-x) = -f(x)\), for every number \(x\) in the domain of \(f\).

blocks.title: Remember!
blocks.text: The graph of an odd function is always symmetric about the origin.

For example: \(f(x) = x^{3}\) is an odd function of \(x\).
Here \(f(-x) = (-x)^{3} = -x = -f(x)\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints \((-x)^{3} = -x\). The cube of \(-x\) is \(-x^{3}\), so the line should read:
\[f(-x) = (-x)^{3} = -x^{3} = -f(x)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Odd means: changing the sign of the input changes only the sign of the output. For \(f(x) = x^{3}\):
\[f(2) = 8, \qquad f(-2) = -8\]
So \((2, 8)\) and \((-2, -8)\) are both on the graph. Turning the graph through half a turn (\(180^{\circ}\)) about the origin brings it onto itself: symmetry about the origin.
The function \(f(\theta) = \cos\theta\) for all \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\) is an even function (see figure 9.2).

Here \(f(-\theta) = \cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta = f(\theta)\).
Thus, \(f(\theta) = \cos\theta\) is an even function.

blocks.alt: Unit circle through (1, 0), (0, 1), (minus 1, 0) and (0, minus 1). Angle theta above the x-axis ends at the point (x, y) = (cos theta, sin theta); angle minus theta below the x-axis ends at its mirror image (x, minus y) = (cos theta, minus sin theta). The two points lie on one vertical line.
blocks.caption: Figure: the angles θ and −θ on the unit circle (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
1. The book refers to "figure 9.2", but there is no such figure in this unit; it means the unit-circle figure printed beside this text (shown above).
2. The lines "The function \(f(\theta) = \cos\theta\) ...", "Thus, \(f(\theta) = \cos\theta\) ..." and the same lines for \(\sin\theta\) below are printed jumbled (the "=" sign and the order of \(\theta\) and \(\cos\) / \(\sin\) are mixed up), and the results print "\(= (\theta)\)" without the letter \(f\). They are written correctly here: \(\cos\theta = f(\theta)\) and \(-\sin\theta = -f(\theta)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\)? Look at the figure. The angle \(-\theta\) is the angle \(\theta\) measured clockwise, so its terminal point is the mirror image of \((x, y)\) in the \(x\)-axis, i.e. \((x, -y)\).
Same \(x\): \(\cos(-\theta) = x = \cos\theta\).
Opposite \(y\): \(\sin(-\theta) = -y = -\sin\theta\).
So one figure proves both results: cosine is even and sine is odd.

Similarly, the function \(f(\theta) = \sin\theta\) for all \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\) is an odd function.
Here \(f(-\theta) = \sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta = -f(\theta)\).
Thus, \(f(\theta) = \sin\theta\) is an odd function.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: In both the cases, for each \(x\) in the domain of \(f\), \(-x\) must also be in the domain of \(f\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why this condition? The tests compare \(f(x)\) with \(f(-x)\); if \(-x\) were not in the domain, \(f(-x)\) would not exist and there would be nothing to compare. The domain must be symmetric about \(0\).
The other four functions follow from sine and cosine (our addition, using \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\), \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\)):
\[\tan(-\theta) = \dfrac{-\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = -\tan\theta\]
\[\sec(-\theta) = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \sec\theta\]
So \(\cos\) and \(\sec\) are even; \(\sin\), \(\csc\), \(\tan\) and \(\cot\) are odd.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
To decide whether a function is even, odd or neither: replace \(x\) by \(-x\), simplify \(f(-x)\), and compare.
If \(f(-x) = f(x)\): even. If \(f(-x) = -f(x)\): odd. If neither holds (for one value is enough): neither.
Example: \(f(x) = x^{2} + x\) gives \(f(-x) = x^{2} - x\), which is neither \(f(x)\) nor \(-f(x)\). So it is neither even nor odd.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Even: \(f(-x) = f(x)\); graph symmetric about the \(y\)-axis. Example \(x^{2}\), \(\cos\theta\).
2. Odd: \(f(-x) = -f(x)\); graph symmetric about the origin. Example \(x^{3}\), \(\sin\theta\).
3. \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\) and \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\) (mirror image in the \(x\)-axis on the unit circle).
4. For both definitions, \(-x\) must be in the domain whenever \(x\) is.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Thinking that every function is either even or odd. Most functions are neither.
2. Writing \((-x)^{3} = x^{3}\): an odd power keeps the minus sign, \((-x)^{3} = -x^{3}\); an even power removes it, \((-x)^{2} = x^{2}\).
3. Writing \(\cos(-\theta) = -\cos\theta\). Cosine is even: the minus sign disappears.
